title: Affect Regulation
subtitle: Modulating emotion without suppressing experience
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating affect regulation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain affect regulation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in affect regulation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to affect regulation.

sections.explainSimply: Affect regulation includes selecting situations, shifting attention, reappraising, accepting and choosing actions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Trauma can narrow access to flexible strategies, with overcontrol, impulsivity or dissociation emerging under load.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Regulation depends on distributed networks and social context; “top-down versus bottom-up” is a useful simplification, not a strict division.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of affect regulation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need affect regulation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Calmness is not the only marker of effective regulation.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use affect regulation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses affect regulation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Calmness is not the only marker of effective regulation. Evidence classification: established psychological science.
